body.text: Meg Mason is a New Zealand-born, Sydney-based writer whose second novel, Sorrow and Bliss, became an international bestseller and was nominated for the Women’s Prize for Fiction in 2022. Centred on mental illness and sisterly love, it won the British Book Awards 2022 in the Fiction Book of the Year category. Her new book, Sophie, Standing There, tells the story of Sophie Pattison, who works in a production role at literary festivals. When the novel opens, Sophie is struggling in the aftermath of a bad divorce, workplace politics, and estrangement from her best friend. Lonely and cut adrift, she rediscovers the work of a famous writer called Lilac Dunne, reading her obsessively and consuming every interview and podcast.

It is a wonderful novel with a memorable central character and a propulsive plot line that follows Sophie’s obsession and how it all comes to a head. Mason, who worked as a journalist for two decades, has also written a memoir of motherhood as well as a novel about a young mother. She has a warm and funny voice, and her novels often explore the dynamics between women.
Edited excerpts from an interview:
How did this new novel start?

I was writing novel number three and was running out of steam. Then I had to take a break to go to a literary festival, and when I got back and looked at it [the novel], I’m like, oh my gosh, this is so terrible, it’s so boring. Which to me is the biggest crime. And then, mercifully, this character of Sophie came into my mind, encapsulated in the first line of the novel [“The Talent never spoke to Sophie Pattison.”].

I was working at this L-shaped desk at the time. And I thought, I’ll just pivot to this other arm of the desk to write this line down. At the end of the day, I was still there, and I’d written 15,000 words. My fingers were so sore because I’d just been typing solidly for these eight hours. I never went back to the other novel, because Sophie suddenly developed this momentum of her own.
So, the character came to you before the idea of a parasocial relationship. How did you decide on writing about this obsessive reader-writer dynamic?

None of that is really conscious. I don’t know how it would work if you sat down and said, I’m going to write a book about loneliness, parasocial relationships, and the literary world. It would be like you were supplying yourself with a brief, and then everything you did would be to try and bend it to fit this brief.

When I hit a hurdle, and it’s a hard writing day, my tendency is to get really literary and start doing gymnastics of some kind, to be impressive. So I had this little note stuck to my wall that said, “Tell it to him as though you’re tired”, the “him” being my husband. [This is the situation] I’m trying to imagine: if he got home late and I had a story to tell him from the day, I’d [narrate it as if] I’m really tired and just want to get it done as fast as I can. [It means] just get the facts out, [add] a little bit of detail, try and make it interesting, then go to bed.
What kind of pressure did you face after the tremendous success of Sorrow and Bliss?

So much pressure. Sorrow and Bliss wasn’t even meant to come out beyond Australia and New Zealand. And then it went worldwide. I was 43 when all of that happened. A late-in-life baby notwithstanding, you don’t really expect your life to change that dramatically when you’re 43. It meant a whole new career. Suddenly there was a whole raft of publishers and editors. You’ve taken an advance. People know your name, and there’s no sense of protection around what you’re doing. People are waiting for the manuscript and it’s so much pressure. But, at the same time, it’s not helpful for me to think too hard about that.
Both you and your character Sophie came to reading as a hobby later than usual. Can you tell me a little bit about that?

My mother was a great reader. She took us to libraries, read to us all the time. But the habit never established itself. As I became a teenager, my friends were all bookworms, and I sort of reacted against it, because I felt like I couldn’t do it. But then I had to move countries with my parents in the final year of high school. Suddenly I had no friends, and there was nothing else to do but read. So I tried it, and I loved it. It was Emma by Jane Austen, a text that we had to read for school.

It’s rare in my industry to meet a writer who wasn’t a reader growing up. Everybody says they were fabulous readers when they were children. You know how parents laud reading, so you do feel like an outlier if you’re not a reader. I wanted to give it to Sophie, because people seemed interested in the idea that you aren’t necessarily a bookworm from the day you were born—it’s something that you can develop. You just need your gateway book, which, for me, came quite late. Ever since then, I’ve read with the sense of catching up.
How did you transition from being a journalist to being a full-time novelist?

I wrote all three books before this one in the after hours on weekends, and very early in the morning while working full time as a journalist. Sorrow and Bliss was coming out in September, 2020, and I had five jobs on retainer. As soon as the lockdown was declared here, I got fired once every day for five days. I lost every single job I had because they were suspending publication or downsizing.

[The success of Sorrow and Bliss] really saved me, because I sometimes wonder what I would be doing now. I’d been doing [journalism] for 20 years, and I feel like every lifestyle feature I had in me, I had written it.

I think I’d always wanted to do this, but it’s such a lofty thing to claim. To say I want to be a novelist is like saying I want to be a model, I want to be a comedian—that’s for everyone else to decide.
The new book has the author doing a lot of podcasts and interviews. Do you also find yourself having to talk about your own books a lot? Is it enjoyable?

The job is to be alone for a year, and then the job is to be out there for a year. I don’t mind it at all, because I get to meet the people who read the book, who let me do what I do. It would feel tremendously ungrateful to be like, I hate coming to your festival. Or I’m too tired to speak to this journalist who’s interested in writing about my book. This [success] was so late in life for me that none of it feels normal yet. None of it will I ever take for granted, so I don’t mind it in the least.

What readers do, and I know what I do, when you meet one of your heroes, is that you want to tell them something. You want to impart this story or this experience you had with their book. I got to meet Elizabeth Gilbert backstage a little while ago, and I was just like, blah blah blah, and it wasn’t until afterwards that I realised I’d talked at that poor woman for two minutes solid, just telling her what her book meant to me.
Is it fair to say that Australian writing—non-fiction and fiction—is having a big moment right now?

Australian fiction is definitely being taken much more seriously overseas now than it used to be. I am, I suppose, to a degree, an Australian writer, but I don’t write Australian books. To me, an Australian book is about the land, it’s often about the country, it’s about Australian people. Often they’re historical, they may be set in the outback.
Have you been following the controversies around writers using AI? Have you been surprised by the use of AI in the literary world?

I am such a Luddite, so disconnected from technology. I don’t use social media. I find it hilarious that my friends actually use ChatGPT to help them write emails. I’m like, do you want your brain to atrophy? I couldn’t do that because I’d be worried for my own intelligence. Maybe it’s because of the late start I had, but I always want to be learning. I don’t have that much time to get smarter, so I’m not going to let a robot take the precious amount of intelligence I have. Also, did you know that ChatGPT uses so much water every time you search on it? So morally I’m not going there.
What’s next?

I can’t write and be on tour at the same time. It almost feels like it’s not fair on the characters if I’m sneaking off with another set of characters. I couldn’t commit to any other characters until I’ve done my duty [with this book].
Bhavya Dore is a freelance journalist who writes for various Indian and international publications.
